**Class Description:**  
This course teaches the principles of designing, implementing, testing, and debugging medium-sized web applications using both client- and server-side technologies. Students will learn:

* Full website development  
* Web security  
* Data markup languages  
* Server-side scripting technologies  
* Web application interactions with databases  
* Web service architectures  
* Web security (admin, user, and read-only user interactions)

**Course Structure:**  
The class follows an agile team approach, with students divided into 4-person teams. The course is organized into 2-week sprints, and each sprint involves forming a new team and conducting a presentation and review. Assignments require the use of AI for writing code.

**Assignments:**

1. **Tools for Class Evaluation and Presentation Voting**  
2. **Client-Only Project**: Create a project with no server interaction.  
3. **Interactive Infographic**: Consume a public data source to allow navigation and data visualization.  
4. **Storytelling on the Web**: Craft a storytelling project using web technologies.  
5. **AI-Powered Project**: Leverage AI from a preselected list or your own choice.

**Presentations:**  
Each team will present their work with a 15-minute presentation, including:

* **Demo**: Showcase your work.  
* **Process Used**: Discuss the development process and highlight how AI was utilized.  
* **Technical Review**: Exhibit the code and explain the implementation.  
* **Retrospective**: Reflect on improvements and lessons learned.  
* **Q\&A**: Answer questions from peers and instructors.

Cheating, Plagiarism Policy & Artificial Intelligence Use (AI Use)

The purpose of education is learning. Learning happens by honest effort; there are no shortcuts. Your role is (and will be, in your professional life) to understand tools and concepts and to use them to solve practical problems. 

When you submit work, you are claiming that it is your own work and that you understand how and why it works. It is appropriate to use external resources, including web sites and other students, to identify useful tools and concepts and to learn how to use them. It is not appropriate to copy work from external resources, regardless of how little of the work is copied. Uploading code to a website that makes it available to others is plagiarism, whether or not you intend to make it available. Do not read another student's code unless explicitly authorized. If you are unsure about what is or is not acceptable, ask your instructor.

Use ChatGPT (or other similar platforms) as a learning assistant, not as a crutch. If you use it, cite it at the top of your code. You are responsible to make sure that any code or content does what it is supposed to do and says what you want it to say. Don't accept anything it generates at face value without checking it critically. These days potential employers will expect you to know how to use tools like ChatGPT to generate code, so it is a skill we need to teach you. If it helps you learn some things faster, GREAT because we can spend class time on more interesting topics. Just remember: If you REALLY want to be good, work for it.
